title: Florida's vaccination coverage has already fallen below the measles herd immunity threshold
dek: Florida's child MMR vaccination rate is only 91.6%, already below the measles herd immunity threshold; removing mandates could push it to 82%, turning measles into an endemic regional disease over fifty years.
why: Two PNAS papers with high information density—the first on measles modeling with actionable policy insights, the second on HLA with controversial but methodologically rich discussion worth careful listening.
who: Public health professionals focused on vaccine policy and infectious disease modeling; anyone interested in SARS-CoV-2 immune escape mechanisms and statistical inference methods.
skip: Listener mail and weekly recommendations (approximately 1:21:50 onward) are unrelated to the two papers and can be skipped.

points.h: Florida's current vaccination coverage already falls below the herd immunity threshold
points.body: The research team created a Florida-specific age-structured transmission model plotting vaccination reproduction number as a heat map, with adult vaccination rate on the x-axis and child vaccination rate on the y-axis. A V-HIT boundary line separates regions where transmission can be stopped from regions where outbreaks occur. Florida's actual vaccination composition (91.6% children) is marked with a star that falls on the red side of the boundary—meaning even without removing any vaccine mandates, Florida's current vaccination coverage is already insufficient to block measles transmission.

points.h: Vaccinating children is ten times more effective per dose than vaccinating adults
points.body: The paper recalculated effectiveness based on vaccination reproduction number (R_v) reduction per dose: increasing child vaccination rate by 1 percentage point reduces R_v by 4%. Per-dose calculations show vaccinating one child reduces R_v by approximately 1×10⁻⁶, while vaccinating one adult reduces it by only 3×10⁻⁷—nearly a tenfold difference. Since the adult population is five times larger than the child population, achieving the same effect through adult vaccination would require vastly more vaccine doses. This explains why school entry vaccine mandates target children.

points.h: Mandate removal could push vaccination rates down to 82 percent within years
points.body: National surveys show 16% of parents distrust MMR vaccine safety, 17% believe risks outweigh benefits, and 18% oppose school entry mandates. Based on these figures, the paper estimates that removing mandates could reduce Florida's child MMR vaccination rate by up to 18 percentage points, down to approximately 82%. Simulating this scenario, Florida would experience a major measles outbreak within 3 to 5 years, with peak incidence rates (260 to 315 cases per 100,000 children) exceeding any year in the US since 1977.

points.h: Adult booster campaigns could restore herd immunity—if children's rates don't also fall
points.body: If child vaccination rate remains at 91% while adult MMR coverage is raised from 92.5% to 96.5% (vaccinating approximately 1 million more adults), simulations show vaccination reproduction number could theoretically drop below 1, maintaining Florida's measles elimination status. However, this rescue plan depends entirely on child vaccination rates not declining further. In reality, adults show poor compliance even with recommended vaccines like influenza and shingles; large-scale adult measles vaccination is unrealistic, and once child rates also start declining, this pathway fails completely.

points.h: Masks and isolation cannot provide the long-term protection vaccines offer
points.body: The paper also simulated non-pharmaceutical interventions: isolation after rash onset and school masking triggered by cases. However, the 80% mask efficacy assumption assumes healthcare workers carefully wearing proper masks during flu season—clearly too optimistic for elementary schoolchildren in practice. Real-world compliance is poor, with adults themselves often wearing masks on their chins. Moreover, even if these interventions worked, they could only manage one outbreak; each subsequent outbreak would require repeated isolation and masking. Unlike vaccination, which provides enduring protection, these measures cannot substitute for it.

points.h: Population MHC diversity prevents single viral variants from eliminating humanity
points.body: This paper challenges a textbook assumption: that T-cell epitope changes from SARS-CoV-2 infection only matter to infected individuals. The conventional thinking is that because each person has different HLA molecules, amino acid changes allowing the virus to escape one person's T-cell recognition become a burden when transmitted to someone with different HLA, getting quickly cleared and not spreading. The paper shows statistically that 69% of SARS-CoV-2 protein amino acid variants fall on CTL epitopes and argues this suggests immune escape mutations might actually persist and spread at the population level.

points.h: Escape mutations spread 1.7 to 2 times faster among common HLA variants
points.body: The paper's strongest evidence comes from comparing the prevalence of T-cell epitope mutations that cause HLA-binding escape across different countries. Results show that escape mutations targeting common HLA alleles appear 1.7 to 2 times more frequently than mutations targeting rare HLA alleles, with this pattern consistent in Delta and post-Omicron data. However, the host notes that correlation alone does not prove selection pressure is at work; the analysis still lacks phylogenetic context capable of ruling out alternative explanations.

points.h: The same correlation pattern misled HIV research until founder effects were discovered
points.body: Brianne recalls a nearly identical episode from HIV research: a 2002 Science paper similarly claimed to find evidence of T-cell escape mutations following HLA allele frequency distribution at the population level. Later researchers re-examined the data using more rigorous founder-virus transmission analysis and found all variation could be explained by founder effects (genetic drift); 2007 publications showed natural selection was not at play. She argues this SARS-CoV-2 paper has the same gap—lacking phylogenetic context to rule out founder effects—so the current evidence cannot yet be considered conclusive.
